items.title: The smaller die
items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. $M$ is the smaller of the two numbers.
items.question: What is $P(M = 2)$?

options.why: You treated the six values of $M$ as equally likely.
You counted every cell with a 2. In (2, 1) the smaller die is 1.
That is $P(M \ge 2)$: both dice at least 2. Take away the cells where both are at least 3.

feedback.generic: Count the cells where both dice are at least 2 and one of them is exactly 2.

explain.text: Both dice at least 2 is a 5 by 5 square, 25 cells. Both at least 3 is 16 cells. The difference, 9 cells, has smaller die exactly 2, so $P(M = 2) = \tfrac{9}{36} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

items.title: Heads in four tosses
items.prose: A fair coin is tossed four times. $X$ is the number of heads. Each of the 16 sequences has chance $\tfrac{1}{16}$.
items.question: Fill in the pmf of $X$.

feedback.generic: Count the sequences with each number of heads: choose where the heads go.

byKey.r1c1: One head can go in any of 4 places.
byKey.r3c1: Three heads means one tail, which can go in any of 4 places.

explain.text: The number of sequences with $k$ heads is $\binom{4}{k}$: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. Over 16 they add to 1.

items.title: The smaller die, at most 2
items.prose: Two fair dice; $M$ is the smaller number.
items.question: What is $F_M(2) = P(M \le 2)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: The smaller die is at most 2 unless both dice are at least 3.

byKey.both: That is the chance both dice are at most 2. One die at most 2 is enough.
byKey.values: You treated the six values as equally likely: 2 of 6.

explain.text: $M > 2$ exactly when both dice are at least 3: $\tfrac{16}{36}$. So $F_M(2) = 1 - \tfrac{16}{36} = \tfrac{20}{36}$. In general $F_M(m) = 1 - \left(\tfrac{6 - m}{6}\right)^2$.

items.title: The pmf of the larger die
items.prose: Two fair dice show $D_1$ and $D_2$, and $Y = \max(D_1, D_2)$. We want $P(Y = y) = \dfrac{2y - 1}{36}$ for $y = 1, \dots, 6$.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\{Y \le y\} = \{D_1 \le y\} \cap \{D_2 \le y\}$: the larger is at most $y$ exactly when both are
$P(Y \le y) = P(D_1 \le y)\,P(D_2 \le y)$: the dice are independent
$= \dfrac{y}{6} \cdot \dfrac{y}{6} = \dfrac{y^2}{36}$: each die is at most $y$ on $y$ of its 6 faces
$P(Y = y) = F(y) - F(y - 1)$: the pmf is the jump of the CDF at $y$

feedback.generic: Find the CDF of $Y$ first, then take its jumps.

explain.text: The CDF comes from both dice being at most $y$, which independence turns into $\tfrac{y^2}{36}$. The pmf is the jump at $y$: $\tfrac{y^2 - (y-1)^2}{36} = \tfrac{2y - 1}{36}$, giving 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 over 36.

items.title: A three-day call
items.prose: In the price model a share moves $+£2$ with chance 0.3, $£0$ with 0.5 and $-£2$ with 0.2 each day, independently. It starts at £100. A call struck at £102 pays $\max(S - 102, 0)$ after three days.
items.question: What is the chance the call pays anything?

feedback.generic: The call pays only if $S > 102$. List the three-day changes that get there.

byKey.forgot-top: You found $P(S = 104)$. Three rises, to £106, also pay.
byKey.one-path: That is one path, up, up, flat. The flat day can be any of the three.
byKey.at-strike: You included $S = 102$, where the call pays $\max(0, 0) = 0$.

explain.text: The call pays when $S$ is £104 or £106. £104 needs two rises and a flat day in some order: $3 \times 0.3^2 \times 0.5 = 0.135$. £106 needs three rises, 0.027, so the chance is 0.162.

items.title: VaR on a jump
items.prose: Another desk's daily loss $L$ in £ thousands has this pmf and CDF. The 95% VaR is the smallest $x$ with $F(x) \ge 0.95$.
items.question: What is the 95% VaR, in £ thousands?

feedback.generic: Find the first row where $F$ is at least 0.95.

byKey.strict: You needed $F$ to pass 0.95. The rule is $F(x) \ge 0.95$, and $F(4) = 0.95$ already meets it.

explain.text: $F(2) = 0.87$ and $F(4) = 0.95$. The rule asks for $F(x) \ge 0.95$, so equality counts and the VaR is £4k.

items.title: A remainder
items.prose: Two fair dice, with $X$ the total. $R$ is the remainder when $X$ is divided by 3, so $R$ is 0, 1 or 2.
items.question: Which is the pmf of $R$?

options.why: You counted the totals that give each remainder as if the 11 totals were equally likely.
You kept only one total for $R = 1$. Totals 4, 7 and 10 all leave remainder 1.
You took one total per remainder. Several totals merge into each value of $R$.

feedback.correct: Each remainder collects 12 of the 36 cells.
feedback.generic: Group the totals by remainder and add their cell counts.

items.title: The larger die, start to finish
items.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and $Y$ is the larger number. (a) Find the CDF $F(y) = P(Y \le y)$ for $y = 1, \dots, 6$, and say what $F$ is below 1 and above 6. (b) Find the pmf of $Y$ from the CDF and check that it adds to 1. (c) A bet pays $Z = \max(Y - 4, 0)$ pounds. Find the pmf of $Z$.
items.model:
**(a)** $Y \le y$ exactly when both dice are at most $y$. That is a $y$ by $y$ square of the 36 equally likely cells, so $$F(y) = \frac{y^2}{36}, \qquad y = 1, \dots, 6.$$ Between whole numbers $F$ is flat. Below 1, $F = 0$, since $Y$ is never below 1. From 6 on, $F = 1$, since $Y \le 6$ always.

**(b)** The pmf is the jump at each value: $p(y) = F(y) - F(y - 1) = \dfrac{y^2 - (y-1)^2}{36} = \dfrac{2y - 1}{36}$. So $p = \tfrac{1}{36}, \tfrac{3}{36}, \tfrac{5}{36}, \tfrac{7}{36}, \tfrac{9}{36}, \tfrac{11}{36}$. Check: $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36$, so the pmf adds to $\tfrac{36}{36} = 1$.

**(c)** $g(y) = \max(y - 4, 0)$ sends 1, 2, 3, 4 to 0, 5 to 1 and 6 to 2. Values that merge add their chances:

- $P(Z = 0) = p(1) + p(2) + p(3) + p(4) = F(4) = \tfrac{16}{36} = \tfrac{4}{9}$
- $P(Z = 1) = p(5) = \tfrac{9}{36} = \tfrac{1}{4}$
- $P(Z = 2) = p(6) = \tfrac{11}{36}$

Check: $16 + 9 + 11 = 36$.

rubric.text: Explains that $Y \le y$ means both dice are at most $y$, giving $F(y) = \tfrac{y^2}{36}$.
States $F = 0$ below 1, $F = 1$ from 6 on, and that $F$ is flat between whole numbers.
Finds the pmf as the jump $F(y) - F(y - 1) = \tfrac{2y - 1}{36}$ and lists all six values.
Checks that the pmf adds to 1.
Applies $g$ to the values: 1 to 4 go to 0, 5 to 1 and 6 to 2.
Adds the merged chances: $P(Z = 0) = \tfrac{16}{36}$, with $P(Z = 1) = \tfrac{9}{36}$ and $P(Z = 2) = \tfrac{11}{36}$.
Checks that the pmf of $Z$ adds to 1.

items.title: A pmf from any sample space
items.prose: In Python a sample space can be a dict: each outcome is a key, and its chance is the value. The chances may be ints, floats or `Fraction`s, and they need not be equal. A random variable is a function `X` that gives each outcome a number.
items.question: Write `pmf_of(space, X)`, which returns the pmf of `X` as a dict `{value: chance}`. Outcomes that share a value add their chances. Leave out any value whose chance is 0. Check the chances first: raise `ValueError` if any chance is negative, or if they do not add up to 1 to within `1e-9`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. A returned pmf must have exactly the right values as its keys, and each chance is compared within rounding (`math.isclose`).

feedback.correct: Your function checks the chances, then adds the chance of every outcome into the value it gets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the first failing test, list its outcomes and values by hand, and compare with what your function returns.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that the `...` is replaced and that every name is defined.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a spinner whose colours are not equally likely. Add each outcome's own chance, not a count of outcomes.
byKey.test-4: If your function raised `ValueError` here, compare the total with 1 within `1e-9`. Ten float chances of 0.1, added one at a time, come to `0.9999999999999999`.
byKey.test-7: If your function raised `ValueError` here, compare the total with 1 within `1e-9`. These float chances add up to `0.9999999999999998`, even with `sum`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has an outcome of chance 0. Its value, 5, never happens, so it is left out of the pmf.
byKey.test-9: Test 9's chances add up to 0.9999. That is more than `1e-9` from 1, so the function should raise `ValueError`.
byKey.test-10: Test 10's chances add up to 1, but one of them is negative. A chance can never be negative, so raise `ValueError`.

explain.text:
The two checks are the two rules every pmf obeys: no negative chance, and a total of 1. Comparing the total with 1 within `1e-9` stops float rounding, such as ten 0.1s, from raising by mistake. Then each outcome adds its chance to the entry for its value, which merges outcomes that share a value.
